questions.q: What makes a token different from an encrypted value, per this lesson?
options: A token has no mathematical relationship to the original value and can only be reversed via a vault lookup, unlike encryption which is mathematically reversible with a key
A token and an encrypted value are functionally identical in every way
A token is always longer than the original value, while ciphertext is always shorter
Tokens can only be used on numeric data, never on text
questions.explain: The lesson emphasizes that you cannot compute your way from a token back to the original value — the only path is looking it up in the token vault, unlike ciphertext which inherently encodes the original data.

options: The tightly controlled system that maps tokens back to their real values
A type of encryption algorithm used for data at rest
A publicly accessible table listing all tokenized values
A synonym for a database role
questions.explain: The vault is the only place the token-to-real-value mapping exists, and it must be protected with the same rigor as the sensitive data it stands in for.

questions.q: How does pseudonymization typically differ from tokenization in how it's applied, according to this lesson?
options: Pseudonymization is typically applied across a whole record or dataset so analysts can see patterns, while tokenization is usually about one isolated value like a card number
Pseudonymization can never be reversed under any circumstances
Tokenization is only used for names, while pseudonymization is only used for card numbers
There is no meaningful difference between the two techniques
questions.explain: The lesson's example has Customer 48213 consistently becoming Patient-X92 across an entire dataset, preserving relationships between records while hiding the real identity.

questions.q: Why does GDPR treat pseudonymized data as still personal data, while anonymized data generally falls outside the regulation?
options: Pseudonymized data is reversible by someone holding the separate mapping, while truly anonymized data has no mapping to reverse at all
GDPR does not distinguish between pseudonymization and anonymization
Anonymized data is always encrypted, while pseudonymized data never is
Pseudonymized data is always stored outside the EU
questions.explain: The lesson explains that if you can get back to the original value by any legitimate path, it's pseudonymization, not anonymization — which is exactly why GDPR still classifies it as personal data, just lower-risk.

questions.q: What do tokenization and pseudonymization both depend on, per this lesson's closing point?
options: The vault or mapping table being protected with the same rigor as the sensitive data it stands in for
Both require the data to be deleted after 90 days
Both require the use of SQL Server's Dynamic Data Masking feature
Neither technique requires any access controls on the mapping
questions.explain: An unsecured vault or an unprotected mapping table provides no real protection — it just relocates the sensitive data to a second place that now also needs defending.
